course.title: Data Science 100
course.description: DS-100 exemplar snapshot generated from course source markdown.

topics.title: Course workflow, weekly learning rhythm, and due-date habits.
Academic integrity, AI-use expectations, and responsible AI collaboration.
Course platforms, assignment workflow, and support channels.
Notebook setup and basic notebook execution.
Notebook operations: running cells, restarting kernels, and reading notebook state.
Troubleshooting common setup, environment, and access errors.
GitHub Classroom credentials and common access recovery steps.
Learning by asking and answering questions.
AI collaboration through follow-up questions, requested reasoning, and checks on first responses.
Local development environments beyond the standard course setup.
Variables and assignment.
Basic data types: integers, floats, strings, and booleans.
Type conversion and type mismatch debugging.
Basic number-system intuition.
Lists as a way to collect related values together, with indexed access.
Functions with parameters and return values.
Conditional logic with `if`, `elif`, and `else`.
Iteration with `for` loops.
Basic debugging habits in notebooks.
Importing libraries and using standard aliases.
DataFrames as tables: data organized in labeled rows and columns.
Creating DataFrames from dictionaries and CSV files.
Basic DataFrame exploration with `.head`, `.shape`, `.info`, and `.describe`.

Selecting rows and columns with column selection, `.loc`, and `.iloc` — including what each name is short for (`.loc` = label-/location-based selection, `.iloc` = integer-location-based selection) and when to reach for which.
List slicing, kept as advanced programming because it appears in real notebooks but is not part of the intro core.
Advanced list methods such as `.index` and `.count`.
`while` loops and loop control.
Function documentation with docstrings.
Number systems: binary, octal, decimal, and hexadecimal — place value, base conversion, and why computers use them (extends LM01-C04).
Using tables and tabular data structures to organize evidence.
Observations, variables, rows, and columns.
Data science workflow: ask a question, prepare data, analyze patterns, and communicate findings.
Recognizing categorical, numerical, and coded variables.
Finding missing values.
Basic cleaning with `.dropna`, `.fillna`, `.astype`, and `pd.to_numeric`.
Duplicate detection and removal.
Finding bad values, impossible values, and suspicious ranges.
Claims, evidence, uncertainty, and limitations.
Association, causation, confounding, and why randomized comparisons matter.
Public data sources, including civic, census, survey, and administrative data.
Basic text cleaning and filtering with `.str` methods such as `.str.lower`, `.str.strip`, and `.str.contains`.
Data dictionaries and metadata quality.
Reproducible cleaning notes and audit trails.
Advanced text processing: regular expressions, `.str.extract`, and multi-step text pipelines.
Boolean filtering and column selection for analysis questions.
Sorting with `.sort_values`.
Summary statistics: mean, median, sum, count, mode, and `value_counts`.
Grouping and aggregation with `.groupby`.
Multi-column grouping and tidy summary tables.
Resetting indexes after grouped summaries.
Basic charts: bar charts, line charts, scatter plots, and histograms.
Chart choice as an analytical decision.
Interpreting charts precisely and connecting patterns to claims.
Reading two-way summary tables.
Joining tables using matching columns.
Checking joins by choosing keys and checking row counts.
Box plots, subplots, and chart customization.
Pivot tables and reshaping data.
Concatenating compatible tables.
Systematic exploratory data analysis walkthroughs.
Histograms, bins, density, and distribution shape.
Center and spread using appropriate measures.
Comparing distributions.
Outliers and their effects on summaries.
Histogram area as percent and height as density.
Choosing summaries that match a distribution.
Describing variation in context.
Standard deviation as a typical distance from the average.
Standard units as distance from average.
Chebyshev's inequality: for any distribution, the proportion of values within a given number of SDs of the average is at least 1 − 1/z².

Normal (bell-shaped) distributions and normal proportions: the 68-95-99.7 rule as a description of how values cluster around the average when a data distribution is bell-shaped (distinct from the sampling-distribution normal approximation / CLT, which is LM05-C16).
Variance and formal spread calculations.
Box plots and other compact distribution summaries.
Sampling with chance, sampling without chance, and convenience samples.
Sampling bias and limits of generalization.
Basic probability ideas for repeated random processes.
Simulation with random choice.
Probability distributions and empirical distributions.
Long-run behavior and simulation stability.
Lists or arrays of simulation results.
Parameters and statistics.
Sampling distributions: how sample results vary.
Resampling from one sample to estimate uncertainty.
Bootstrap distributions: simulated variation from resampling.
Percentiles.
Confidence intervals.
Interpreting confidence intervals and recognizing common misinterpretations.
Cases where bootstrap methods are inappropriate or fragile.

The Central Limit Theorem, stated not derived: for a large random sample drawn with replacement, the distribution of the sample average is approximately bell-shaped regardless of the population shape, centered at the population mean, with spread equal to the population SD over the square root of the sample size.

Normal-based confidence interval for a mean, used as a shortcut of about the mean plus or minus 2 SDs of the sample-average distribution, with the bootstrap kept as the general method for any other statistic.
Sample-size effects: larger samples give less variable estimates and narrower intervals, following the square-root-of-n rule.
Checking whether the data fit a proposed explanation.
Null and alternative hypotheses.
Test statistics.
Simulating outcomes under a null model.
P-values as tail probabilities under a null model.
Statistical significance and practical significance.
Type I and Type II errors by example.
A/B testing design and critique.
Shuffling group labels to simulate no treatment effect.
Random assignment as the basis for stronger causal claims.
Causal caution when data are observational or groups were not randomly assigned.
Bias, confounding, missingness, and measurement problems that can make a test untrustworthy.
Total variation distance for comparing categorical distributions.
Multiple testing and false discovery.
Testing examples involving digit distributions or other unusual null models.
Association between numerical variables.
Correlation.
Standard units: values measured by distance from average.
Prediction as an analytical task.
Linear regression model fitting.
Interpreting regression slope and intercept.
Prediction error and residuals.
Root mean squared error as "how far off predictions usually are."
Residual plots, model limitations, and checking whether a linear model is appropriate.
Nearest-neighbor prediction.
Classification concepts and tradeoffs.
Nearest-neighbor classification.
Training data, validation data, and checking predictions on data not used to build the model.
Ethics, bias, and harms in modeling.
Least squares as the idea that the regression line is the one that makes the prediction errors as small as possible, taught as a concept rather than a formal minimization or derivation.
Feature engineering.
More than one predictor.
Classification metrics beyond accuracy.
Communicating results to nontechnical audiences.
Matching claims to evidence and limitations.
Explaining uncertainty in plain language.
Presenting an independent analysis.
Reproducible project packaging.
Slide or poster design for data communication.
